FOR INDEPENDENT CATASTROPHE (CAT) CLAIMS ADJUSTERS

A good per-claim rate can still be a bad trip.

A fee schedule that pays $550 a claim reads well right up until the estimating-software, lodging, per diem, vehicle cost, and the unpaid days spent driving to and from the disaster zone come out. This free calculator finds real net profit for one deployment, then lets you compare two or three IA firms' offers by what they actually pay per hour — not their headline per-claim rate.

Everything on this page runs in your browser and nothing is ever uploaded. Your deployment inputs (days, pace, fee schedule, daily costs) are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them next time — Reset to defaults clears them, and Copy shareable link puts them in a URL fragment your browser never sends anywhere. Your fee-schedule comparison rows are a different promise: they are never saved anywhere, and closing or refreshing the tab clears them. There is no account. We count only anonymous local feature events (deployment-priced, offers-compared, link-copied, reset) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no firm names, fees, or deployment figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Fee schedule looks fine on paper — is it actually worth it?

A $550-a-claim offer can still pay under $3 an hour once a slow pace and the full trip's costs are netted out. Is this CAT adjuster fee schedule worth it? works through the arithmetic on a real lowball offer next to a solid one.

Common questions

Why does the per-claim fee alone not tell me whether a deployment is worth it?

Because the per-claim fee only pays for claims you actually close, and closing them depends on a pace you cannot fully control. Meanwhile estimating-software, lodging, per diem, vehicle, and mileage cost accrue every day you are away from home, including the unpaid travel days spent driving to and from the disaster zone before your first claim closes. A fee schedule can look generous per claim and still pay a low effective hourly rate once the full trip's costs and a realistic pace are netted out.

Does this tool tell me whether I'm licensed or appointed to work a deployment?

No. This calculator only prices your own deployment economics from numbers you supply. It does not determine your licensing, appointment, or authority to handle a claim in any state, and it does not evaluate an IA firm's reputation, timeliness of payment, or claim-volume promises -- verify those independently before accepting a deployment.

Why do unpaid travel days count toward the cost but not the claims?

Because that is what actually happens on a deployment: you are paying for lodging, food, your estimating-software subscription, and your vehicle on the days you drive to and from the disaster zone, but you are not closing claims on those days. Leaving travel days out of the cost side is the most common way a deployment's real profit gets overstated.

Does anything about my deployment or fee schedule get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the fee-schedule offers you type into the comparison table are never saved anywhere -- they exist only in the page while it is open. The deployment inputs above are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

is-this-cat-adjuster-fee-schedule-worth-.text:
← Back to the deployment profit calculator

Is this CAT adjuster fee schedule worth it?

Two independent-adjusting (IA) firms both offer a 21-working-day deployment, both with the same 2 unpaid travel days and the same daily costs — an estimating-software subscription, a hotel room, per diem, a vehicle, and mileage between claims. The only real difference is the fee schedule and the pace each firm's claim volume actually supports. Run both through the calculator and the gap is not close.

Firm A: $550 a claim, 1.5 claims a day

21 working days at 1.5 claims/day is 31.5 claims, 10% of them large-loss and worth a $400 bonus on top of the $550 base — a blended $590 a claim.

LineAmount
Gross revenue (31.5 claims, blended $590/claim)$18585.00
In-zone daily cost × 21 days−$5052.60
Travel-day cost × 2 days−$374.00
Fixed deployment cost (E&O / license / dues share)−$150.00
Net profit$13008.40
Effective rate$61.94/hr worked, $565.58/day over the full 23-day trip

A 70.0% profit margin and $412.97 profit per claim. This is a deployment worth taking, and the effective hourly rate confirms it rather than just the headline per-claim fee.

Firm B: $350 a claim, but only 0.8 claims a day

Same 21 working days, same 2 travel days, same daily costs — but this firm's territory only supports 0.8 claims a day (16.8 total, 5% large-loss with a smaller $300 bonus), and the base fee is a third lower.

LineAmount
Gross revenue (16.8 claims, blended $365/claim)$6132.00
In-zone daily cost × 21 days−$5052.60
Travel-day cost × 2 days−$374.00
Fixed deployment cost (E&O / license / dues share)−$150.00
Net profit$555.40
Effective rate$2.64/hr worked, $24.15/day over the full 23-day trip

Notice what did not change: the daily costs are identical, because lodging, food, software, vehicle, and travel days do not care what a firm pays per claim. Only the pace and the fee schedule moved, and together they took the margin from 70.0% down to 9.1% — a profit of $33.06 per claim instead of $412.97, and $555.40 for three full weeks away from home. Firm B's offer never shows a loss on paper. It is still very likely the wrong trip to take, and the only way to see that is to price the whole deployment rather than the fee schedule alone.

The break-even pace tells you how much slack you have

At Firm A's $590 blended fee, the deployment breaks even at just 0.45 claims a day — well under the 1.5/day this scenario assumes, so there is real room for a slow week. At Firm B's $365 blended fee, break-even climbs to 0.73 claims a day — nearly the entire assumed 0.8/day pace, which means almost any slowdown (a storm that weakens, a firm that over-promised volume, a stretch of denied or reassigned claims) tips the whole trip into a loss. A fee schedule with little pace to spare above its own break-even is a materially riskier deployment even before anything goes wrong.

Common questions

Why does Firm B's offer still show a profit if it's a bad deal?

Because none of its daily costs changed -- lodging, food, software, vehicle, and the two unpaid travel days cost the same no matter which firm you work for. Only the pace and the fee schedule moved, and together they cut the margin from 70.0% to 9.1%, which the per-claim fee alone never shows.

What is the fastest way to tell two fee schedules apart?

Compare break-even claims per day, not the per-claim fee. Firm A's schedule breaks even at 0.45 claims a day, well under its assumed 1.5/day pace; Firm B's breaks even at 0.73, nearly its entire assumed 0.8/day pace -- almost no slack for a slow week.

These are worked examples from user-supplied assumptions, not a guarantee any specific IA firm will match them. This page does not determine your licensing, appointment, or authority to handle a claim in any state, and it does not evaluate an IA firm's reputation, timeliness of payment, or claim-volume promises — verify those independently before accepting a deployment.

vs-spreadsheet-comparison.html.text:
← CAT Adjuster Fee Schedule & Deployment Profit Calculator

This calculator vs. comparing fee schedules by spreadsheet or mental math

The arithmetic is the same either way: net profit and effective hourly rate, after daily cost and unpaid travel days come out of the gross. The difference is what happens when that arithmetic gets built from scratch, under time pressure, for a second offer that just came in.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet or mental math can produce exactly the same answer as this calculator — the math is multiplication and subtraction, not anything exotic. What a blank spreadsheet or a phone screen does not give you is a place that already has every line an offer needs: estimating-software cost, lodging, per diem, vehicle, mileage, the large-loss bonus rate, and the two categories of day — in-zone and unpaid travel — that get billed differently. Building that structure correctly once, for one offer, on a deadline between claims, and then building it again identically for a second firm's offer, is where a dropped line or an inconsistent assumption creeps in.

This calculator is that structure already built. Fill in the same fields for each firm's offer and the comparison table applies the same formula to both, so the two offers are judged by the same rules rather than by however carefully each spreadsheet happened to be built that day.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What does this specific offer actually pay per hour?This calculator's deployment profit result — free, private, no account.
Which of two or three offers pays the best effective rate for the same trip?This calculator's fee-schedule comparison table.
My deployment has a rule this calculator doesn't model (a stepped per diem, a shared rental).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
Is this firm reliable, and will it actually assign the claim volume it promised?Neither. Check with other adjusters who have worked for that firm.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a spreadsheet just as accurate as this calculator?

A correctly built one is, because the arithmetic itself is simple multiplication and subtraction. The risk is not the math, it is building it correctly twice: once for each firm's offer, under time pressure, often on a phone between claims. A spreadsheet has no built-in reminder to price the unpaid travel days the same way for both offers, or to apply the same large-loss bonus rate consistently — and a single dropped line changes which offer looks better without showing an error.

When is a spreadsheet actually the better choice?

When the deployment has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a per-diem that steps down after a set number of days, a firm that pays mileage only past a threshold, or a shared rental vehicle split three ways. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that is quick to fill in correctly and hard to get wrong by accident, for the common case of a flat per-claim fee, a large-loss bonus, and steady daily costs.

What does mental math miss that either a spreadsheet or this calculator would catch?

The unpaid travel days, almost every time. It is easy to estimate a per-claim rate against a rough daily cost in your head and get a directionally sane answer, and much harder to also carry two unpaid travel days of full daily cost through that mental estimate without a place to write it down. Both a spreadsheet and this calculator force the travel-day cost onto the page as its own line, which is what actually closes the gap between a fee schedule that looks fine and a deployment that pays a few dollars an hour.

Does this replace comparing IA firms on anything other than price?

No, and it is not built to. This calculator and a spreadsheet both stop at the arithmetic: net profit and effective hourly rate from the numbers you supply. Neither one evaluates a firm's reputation, how reliably it pays, or whether its claim-volume promises for a given storm are realistic — that still has to come from other adjusters' experience with that firm, checked independently before accepting a deployment.

Open the deployment profit calculator, or see a worked example comparing two firms' offers.

vs-the-headline-per-claim-rate.html.text:
← CAT Adjuster Fee Schedule Calculator

This calculator vs. judging an offer by its headline per-claim rate

A $550-a-claim offer and a $350-a-claim offer both look like a rate you can rank on their face. Neither number says what the trip actually pays once pace, daily costs, unpaid travel days, and a blended large-loss bonus come out. This free calculator turns any fee schedule into an effective hourly rate so two offers can be ranked on what they actually pay.

What each one tells you

The headline per-claim rate is the number two IA firms lead with, and it is real — but it is one factor in an hourly figure, not the figure itself. It says nothing about how many claims a day that firm's volume and assignment pattern actually support, and nothing about the lodging, per diem, vehicle, software, and unpaid travel-day cost that run every day in the field regardless of which firm sent you.

This calculator takes the same fee schedule — per-claim fee, large-loss share and bonus — along with your assumed pace and daily costs, and produces the number the rate alone can't: profit per hour actually worked, and the break-even claims-per-day pace below which the deployment loses money. The fee-schedule comparison table runs two or three offers side by side on that same basis.

It exists because a fee schedule that never shows a loss on paper can still pay a few dollars an hour once a slower pace and the same daily costs are counted against it. See a worked example where a $350/claim offer beats a $550/claim offer on paper and loses badly once hours are counted.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which of two fee schedules actually pays more per hour?This calculator's fee-schedule comparison — enter each offer, compare net profit for the same deployment.
What claims-per-day pace do I need just to break even?This calculator's break-even pace figure, from your own daily costs.
Does a bigger large-loss bonus mean a better firm?Only if that firm also assigns enough large-loss claims — enter the bonus and share to see the blended effect.
Should I take this firm's reputation or pay-speed on faith?No — verify those independently. This calculator only prices the fee schedule and pace you enter.
Is my fee-schedule data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; comparison rows are never saved and clear on refresh by design.

This calculator is arithmetic on the fee schedule, pace, and costs you supply. It does not evaluate a firm's reputation, timeliness of payment, or claim-volume promises, and it is not licensing, insurance, or business advice.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Why isn't the per-claim rate enough to compare two offers?

Because it says nothing about pace, and pace is what turns a rate into income. A $550-a-claim firm assigning 0.8 claims a day and a $350-a-claim firm assigning 1.5 a day can land on either side of each other once claims per day are multiplied out — and neither number alone tells you which. The rate is one factor in an hourly figure, not the figure itself.

What do daily costs and travel days change that the per-claim rate can't show?

They are the same regardless of which firm you deploy for, so they shrink a slower firm's margin more than a faster one's. Lodging, per diem, vehicle cost, and an estimating-software subscription run every day in the field, and the unpaid days spent driving to and from the disaster zone add cost with zero claims closed. A fee schedule that never shows a loss on paper can still pay only a few dollars an hour once those costs are counted against a slower pace.

Does a large-loss bonus change which offer actually pays more?

It can, because a bonus that looks identical on two fee schedules is worth different amounts depending on how many large-loss claims each firm actually assigns. A firm that pays a bigger bonus per large-loss claim but assigns fewer of them can blend lower than a firm with a smaller bonus and more large-loss volume — the headline bonus number alone does not say which.

Does this calculator replace comparing firms on reputation or pay speed?

No. It only turns the numbers you enter — fee schedule, assumed pace, and daily costs — into an effective hourly rate for a deployment. It does not evaluate a firm's reputation, how quickly it actually pays, or its claim-volume promises; verify those independently before accepting a deployment.
